paper_title: WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{WeaveVLA}, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $π_{0.5}$, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $π_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained vision-language representations with robot demonstrations to learn instruction-conditioned manipulation policies. Representative approaches such as OpenVLA and OpenVLA-OFT have advanced general-purpose manipulation, while recent systems have expanded these capabilities across robotic embodiments (Kim et al., 2024, 2025; NVIDIA, 2026). Flowbased policies, including π0, π0.5, and π0.7, further advance continuous action generation, generalization, and steerable control (Black et al., 2025b,a; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026). Despite these advances, understanding and maintaining the spatial relationships that govern manipulation remains an important challenge. Robot actions depend on different relative 3D relations at different stages of manipulation. For example, placing cup into bowl requires reasoning about grippercup relations during grasping and cupbowl relations during placement, while other object pairs may be less relevant. These relations change with robot and object motion, while geometric estimation errors, viewpoint changes, and occasional occlusion can make their current configurations difficult to determine reliably (Peng et al., 2026). SpatialVLA and 3DSVLA improve spatial awareness through geometric representations and sequential spatial constraints (Qu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). GraphCoT-VLA and TriRelVLA further explore structured 3D relations for manipulation (Huang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). This raises central question: How can VLA models explicitly model task-relevant 3D relations and continuously update their representations as manipulation unfolds to support action generation? 1 Figure 1: Conceptual comparison of (a) standard VLA, (b) an illustrative fully connected graph-based VLA, and (c) WeaveVLA. Unlike uniform scene-wide connectivity, WeaveVLA selects task-relevant connections and updates pair-specific relational states across observations. To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, framework that explicitly models task-relevant relative 3D relations and their evolution during manipulation to enhance VLA action generation, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Its object-centric representation combines visual features with estimated 3D geometry, using the robots tool center point (TCP) to anchor gripperobject relations. task-conditioned graph connects instruction-relevant objects, the gripper, and nearby spatial references, while edge-aware graph attention encodes their relative 3D geometry. To maintain evolving spatial context, WeaveVLA assigns recurrent state to each selected entity pair and updates it with valid geometric evidence across observations. The resulting relation features are conditioned on the vision-language context and summarized into compact relational tokens. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages the learned relational features to preserve spatial structure. Together with the original vision-language representations, these tokens condition continuous action expert for robot manipulation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on two VLA backbones, StarVLA-GR00T and π0.5, and evaluate its effectiveness on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022). On the four standard LIBERO suites, WeaveVLA achieves average success rates of 98.3% and 98.2%, respectively, improving both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, it improves StarVLA-GR00T from 74.9% to 82.0% and π0.5 from 85.7% to 87.8%, demonstrating consistent gains across the two architectures. On CALVIN DD, WeaveVLA increases the average completed sequence length from 3.645 to 3.910 for StarVLA-GR00T, surpassing the original π0.5 baseline, and from 3.885 to 3.997 for π0.5. Across three real-world tasks, the StarVLAGR00T-based WeaveVLA achieves average success rates of 70.0% under standard conditions and 53.3% under perturbations, outperforming both baselines. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We introduce WeaveVLA, 3D relational grounding framework that explicitly models task-relevant spatial relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references to enhance VLA action generation. 2. We develop pair-specific recurrent relational updating to maintain evolving 3D relations across observations, integrating valid geometric evidence while preserving historical relational context. 3. We demonstrate consistent improvements across two VLA backbones on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN DD, and validate WeaveVLA on three real-world manipulation tasks, outperforming both baselines under standard and OOD conditions. 2 Figure 2: Architecture of WeaveVLA. Object-level visual features and relative 3D geometry form task-conditioned relational graph. Graph Transformer blocks encode and propagate relational features, while pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate valid geometric evidence across observations. Cross-attention incorporates vision-language context, and Q-Former extracts compact relational tokens. The action interface shown is for StarVLA-GR00T.

sections.title: 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models
sections.content: Building on pretrained vision-language representations and robot demonstrations, vision-language-action (VLA) research has advanced toward more generalizable robot manipulation. Early approaches such as RT-2 and OpenVLA demonstrated the transfer of visual-semantic knowledge to robotic control (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). OpenVLA-OFT improved action generation efficiency through continuous action representations, parallel decoding, and action chunking (Kim et al., 2025). Subsequent VLA architectures further advanced continuous action generation and manipulation across diverse tasks (Black et al., 2025b; Bjorck et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026). More recent models have expanded generalization and adaptability, with π0.5 demonstrating generalization to unseen environments (Black et al., 2025a) and π0.7 advancing steerable execution and compositional generalization (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026). LingBot-VLA 2.0 and GR00T N1.7 further advanced cross-embodiment manipulation (Wu et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026), while Gemini Robotics 2 extended generalist control to whole-body and dexterous manipulation. WeaveVLA complements these advances by augmenting VLA action generation with explicit, task-relevant 3D spatial relations.

sections.title: 2.2 Spatial Grounding for Robotic Manipulation
sections.content: Spatial grounding connects visual observations with the geometric structure of the environment to support robotic manipulation. Recent studies have incorporated explicit 3D representations into VLA policies. SpatialVLA introduces 3D positional encoding to enhance spatial awareness (Qu et al., 2025), while 3DS-VLA combines 2D-3D feature alignment with sequential spatial constraints for manipulation (Li et al., 2025). Graph-based representations have also been explored for spatial relation modeling in navigation and autonomous driving, exemplified by BSG and GraphAD (Liu et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2024). Graph-of-Mark further enhances spatial reasoning for multimodal models via graph-based visual prompting (Frisoni et al., 2026). For robotic manipulation, scene graphs have been used for both high-level planning and action conditioning. Compose by Focus employs task-relevant graphs to condition diffusion-based manipulation skills (Qi et al., 2026), while GraSP-VLA uses scene graphs for symbolic planning and policy orchestration (Neau et al., 2025). SIR further learns task-relevant graph sparsification for action generation (Mattes et al., 2026). More directly, GraphCoT-VLA combines an updatable 3D pose-object graph with structured reasoning (Huang et al., 2026), while TriRelVLA models object-hand-task relations to condition action prediction (Zhou et al., 2026). Other studies have explored spatiotemporal representations for manipulation: ConsisVLA-4D addresses spatiotemporal consistency (Li et al., 2026), semantic-geometric 3 task representations jointly encode object relations and motion histories (Herbert et al., 2026), and Qian et al. maintain dynamic scene graphs as structured memory under partial observability (Qian et al., 2026). While these studies demonstrate the value of spatial structure and temporal context, WeaveVLA focuses on explicitly encoding task-relevant relative 3D relations for action generation. task-conditioned graph captures gripperobject and objectreference geometry, while observation-aware recurrent updates maintain pair-specific relational states across observations.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: WeaveVLA grounds robot actions in task-relevant relative 3D relations, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Given RGB observations from the available cameras, proprioception st, and instruction ℓ, the framework associates tracked entities with visual features and estimated 3D geometry. task-conditioned graph organizes relative spatial relations among relevant objects, the gripper, and nearby references, while pair-specific recurrent states maintain these relations across observations. learned-query readout then extracts compact relational tokens from the updated graph features, which complement the original vision-language context Ht to condition continuous action expert.

sections.title: 3.1 Object-Centric Observation Representation
sections.content: To ground 3D spatial relations, WeaveVLA first establishes object-centric visual representations with consistent identities across observations. At episode initialization, an adapted YOLOE detector (Wang et al., 2025) supplies labeled boxes to frozen SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2026); Cutie (Cheng et al., 2024) then propagates instance masks and identities. Robot regions are excluded from object instance masks before feature pooling. Object appearance features are pooled from visual tokens aligned with instance masks in the same camera view, while the original VLM retains its backbone-specific camera inputs. Since visual tokens may only partially overlap an object, we aggregate instance features according to their foreground coverage. For visible instance with nonempty current mask, let aip,t denote its foreground area within visual token grid cell p, with feature fp,t. The instance appearance feature is computed as (cid:88) vi,t = p:aip,t>0 aip,t aiq,t (cid:80) fp,t. (1) The gripper is represented as separate entity. Its finger masks are obtained from robot geometry and camera calibration, and appearance features are pooled from visible finger regions using the same foreground-coverage weighting. Its 3D position is anchored at the calibrated tool center point (TCP), obtained from robot kinematics rather than visual depth. Detector adaptation, mask filtering, and tracking details appear in Appendix E.

sections.title: 3.2 Spatial Graph Construction and Encoding
sections.content: Spatial grounding aligns geometry of tracked objects and the gripper TCP within shared image-aligned coordinate frame. Masked metric depth from DA3Metric-Large (Lin et al., 2025) is backprojected using camera intrinsics, while the calibrated TCP is transformed into the same frame. Stable references help mitigate depth-scale drift under fixed camera, with the correction applied only to estimated object geometry. Node features combine foreground appearance, averaged VLM input embeddings of the category label, and point MLP with max pooling over centered point clouds. Appendix details the geometry-retention rules and graph-attention operations. The instruction and local geometry jointly determine graph connectivity. parser and frozen sentence encoder match instruction phrases to object categories and bind the corresponding candidate instances once per episode. Task candidates connect to one another and to the gripper. Each candidate with current geometric support selects its = 2 nearest currently supported objects, counting existing connections and including unmentioned objects. Selected connections are bidirectional, and eligible object edges can persist during occlusion. Scene nodes with usable geometry can contribute to the readout even if they have no selected edges. 4 For each selected ordered entity pair, we explicitly encode its relative 3D displacement and distance: gij,t = [(cj,t ci,t), cj,t ci,t2], (2) where ci,t denotes the 3D reference position of entity i. The first stage encodes node features and relative 3D geometry, while the second stage propagates relational features after recurrent updating and VLM conditioning. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate how explicit 3D relational grounding enhances StarVLA-GR00T and π0.5 on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a), LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025), and CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022), comparing each WeaveVLA instantiation with its corresponding backbone. We further evaluate the StarVLA-GR00Tbased variant on three real-world manipulation tasks and analyze key design choices and inference latency.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: In benchmark comparisons, red/bold and Dashes denote unavailable results throughout the tables. blue/underlined values indicate the best and second-best scores, including ties. Implementation details. We instantiate WeaveVLA on two VLA backbones, StarVLA-GR00T (Community, 2026) and π0.5 (Black et al., 2025a). The StarVLA-GR00T instantiation uses Qwen3-VL-4BInstruct (Bai et al., 2025) and the QwenGR00T action framework. The relational module has hidden width of 256 and eight attention heads, with two layers each for spatial encoding, VLM-conditioned graph propagation, and learned-query readout. We use 16 relational tokens by default. Backbone-specific training configurations and hyperparameters for each benchmark are provided in Appendix A. 6 Figure 3: Real-robot setup and example task trajectories. (a) The dual-arm platform uses third-person camera for graph construction, high-mounted main camera, and two wrist cameras. (b) Recorded demonstrations of stacking bowls, placing pens in cups, and cleaning the table. Each row shows four chronological frames from single demonstration. LIBERO. LIBERO comprises four suites: Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long, with Long corresponding to LIBERO-10. We evaluate 500 rollouts per suite and report the success rate of each suite and their average. LIBERO-Plus. LIBERO-Plus contains 10,030 perturbed tasks spanning seven perturbation categories. For each model, we reuse its LIBERO-trained checkpoint with unchanged inference settings, without additional training or fine-tuning on LIBERO-Plus. Each perturbed task is evaluated once, and overall success is pooled across all 10,030 trials. Both benchmarks use control-step limits of 220, 280, 300, and 520 for the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites, respectively, with ten settling steps. CALVIN. We evaluate WeaveVLA on CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022) under the DD setting, where models are trained and evaluated in environment using separate training and evaluation sequences. The evaluation consists of 1,000 sequences of five consecutive language-conditioned subtasks, with at most 360 control steps per subtask. We report the success rates for completing at least one through five consecutive subtasks and the average completed sequence length (Avg. Len.). Each instruction is treated as separate graph-state episode, with task bindings and recurrent edge states reset at each subtask transition. Real-world setup. We evaluate three real-world manipulation tasks as shown in Fig. 3. 1) Bowl Stacking. The robot places the first bowl on plate, then uses its position to align and stack the second bowl. 2) Place Pens in Cups. The robot sequentially picks up two pens and places each in its designated cup. 3) Clean Table. The robot hangs the mug on the rack, then places the first paper ball, the block, and the second paper ball in the basket. For each task and method, we conduct 30 trials under standard conditions and 30 out-of-distribution (OOD) trials, evenly split across table clutter, lighting perturbations, and background variations. We report binary task success and stage-wise progress score based on completed stages in the predefined task sequence. Appendix provides detailed task configurations, OOD settings, and progress scoring criteria.

sections.content: Notably, the StarVLA-based variant improves performance across all seven perturbation categories, with substantial gains of 15.4 points under Camera, 9.4 under Noise, 8.9 under Language, and 6.9 under Robot perturbations. The π0.5-based variant achieves gains of 8.2 and 4.1 points under Robot and Camera perturbations, respectively, while reaching 97.9% and 97.4% success under Light and Background perturbations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit 3D relational grounding across diverse perturbations and VLA backbones.

sections.title: 4.3 Real-World Results
sections.content: WeaveVLA builds upon the StarVLA-GR00T backbone (Community, 2026). Figure 4 compares its performance with StarVLA-GR00T and π0.5 (Black et al., 2025a) across three real-world tasks. Standard conditions. WeaveVLA achieves an average success rate of 70.0%, improving on π0.5 and StarVLA-GR00T by 8.9 and 14.4 percentage points, respectively. It succeeds in 90.0% of bowl-stacking trials and 73.3% of pen-placement trials, while table cleaning remains the most challenging task at 46.7%. OOD conditions. WeaveVLA achieves an average success rate of 53.3%, compared with 41.1% for π0.5 and 33.3% for StarVLA-GR00T. Notably, although the original StarVLA-GR00T underperforms π0.5, its WeaveVLA-enhanced variant surpasses π0.5 under both conditions. It improves success across all three tasks, with the largest gain over StarVLA-GR00T on bowl stacking. WeaveVLA also achieves the highest mean progress score on each task under both conditions. On OOD pen placement, it completes 3.3 of four stages on average, compared with 3.0 for π0.5 and 2.9 for StarVLA-GR00T. Across the three tasks, WeaveVLA achieves 46.7% success under table clutter, 50.0% under random lighting, and 63.3% under background variation. Its gains over π0.5 are 3.3 percentage points under clutter and 16.7 points under each of the other perturbations. Table 10 in the appendix reports the breakdown by task and method.

sections.title:
4.4.2 Error Analysis of Relative Geometry
We analyze geometric estimation errors for absolute object positions and pairwise relative displacements
using selected LIBERO-Plus trajectories. Both are computed from identical depth predictions and instance
masks.
sections.content: As shown in Fig. 5, relative displacements exhibit substantially lower geometric errors, reducing the RMSE by 53.6%. This reduction is consistent with the partial cancellation of shared localization biases between objects, making relative geometry less sensitive to common position errors without requiring more accurate depth estimates.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We have introduced WeaveVLA, framework that enhances VLA models by explicitly encoding taskrelevant relative 3D relations and modeling their evolution throughout manipulation. By combining task-conditioned sparse graph construction with pair-specific recurrent relational updating, WeaveVLA integrates current spatial geometry and historical relational context for continuous action generation. Extensive evaluations on simulation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements across different VLA backbones, highlighting the effectiveness of explicit relational grounding for robotic manipulation. On three real-world tasks, WeaveVLA improves success over both baselines under standard and perturbed conditions.

sections.title: B Implementation Details
sections.content: WeaveVLA maintains graph states using tracked instance identities and ordered entity pairs. Newly observed node features replace cached values, while eligible historical features are retained when observations are missing. shared GRU maintains separate recurrent states for each ordered pair, initialized to zero for unseen pairs. These states persist across observations but are detached between updates. They are reset when the geometric reference changes, and expire 64 control steps after the last valid update. 15 Geometric validity is determined by observation consistency and the age of retained information. Static-geometry consistency is assessed using mask IoU, mask-centroid displacement, relative mask-area change, and mean absolute RGB difference within an eroded common mask region, with respective thresholds of 0.85, 1.5 pixels at 224-pixel reference scale, 15%, and 8 intensity units. Depth-scale correction requires two confirmations and at least two reliable reference objects. The correction factor is clipped to [0.8, 1.25] and can be retained for up to 16 control steps. Occluded object geometry may remain available for 64 control steps under fixed calibration, subject to clearance from the gripper. The TCP remains independent of depth-scale correction. Retained geometry can contribute to spatial encoding, but only valid geometric support permits recurrent updates, as defined in Eq. (6). Instance appearance features are obtained through foreground-coverage pooling, as described in Eq. (1). Training and inference use identical pooling operations on backbone-specific visual token grids. For StarVLA, Qwen3-VL resizes 224 224 images to 256 256, yielding an 8 8 post-merger token grid, while π0.5 uses 16 16 SigLIP patch grid. Masks are aligned with their visual tokens, and foreground coverage determines the pooling weights. When instance masks or visible finger regions are unavailable, the corresponding current visual features are set to zero, while eligible historical node features are retained. The initial node representation combines category semantics, local point-cloud geometry, and pooled appearance features: h(0) i,t = ϕV (cid:16) Wℓsℓ pi,t Wvvi,t (cid:17) , (11) where sℓ Here denotes concatenation and ϕV is an MLP. denotes the category embedding, pi,t the point-cloud feature, and vi,t the pooled visual feature. Graph connectivity follows the task-conditioned construction described in Sec. 3.2. Each currently supported task object selects up to = 2 nearest objects as local references. Existing task connections count toward this limit, and duplicate edges do not introduce additional neighbors. Selected relations are bidirectional, while eligible historical edges may persist during temporary occlusion. Both graph-attention stages use edge-dependent attention biases and message embeddings, as defined in Eqs. (3) and (4). Attention is restricted to selected neighbors and self-connections, with zero edge contributions for self-attention. Multiple heads are concatenated before output projection and residual feed-forward updates. Directed edge features are updated using the input features of their two endpoints and their previous edge representations (Eq. (5)). Sparse connectivity restricts message propagation, although attention is implemented using masked dense tensors. In WeaveVLA, Q-Former uses learned queries to aggregate usable node features and selected edge features into fixed number of relational tokens. For StarVLA, relational tokens are appended to the original VLM cross-attention context, preserving its attention mask. For π0.5, the projected relational tokens are inserted before the noisy action tokens, allowing the action expert to attend to both relational information and the original vision-language prefix.

sections.title: E Perception Adaptation
sections.content: Instance masks are used to construct graph nodes and pool foreground features. We obtain these masks by using YOLOE bounding boxes to prompt frozen SAM 3 model. To improve instance coverage within each benchmark, we fine-tune separate YOLOE detectors for LIBERO and CALVIN D-to-D using simulator-derived supervision. We evaluate both the detector outputs and the resulting SAM 3 masks to assess how detector adaptation affects the perception input to the graph module. Figure 6: Qualitative comparison of instance segmentation on LIBERO (top) and CALVIN scene (bottom). Columns show RGB observations, simulator ground-truth masks, and masks produced by the same frozen SAM 3 model using bounding boxes from the original and fine-tuned YOLOE detectors. Fine-tuning recovers previously missed instances, including the plate and cookie box in LIBERO and cabinet components in CALVIN. Simulator states provide paired static-camera RGB observations and visible-instance masks for detector supervision. For LIBERO, the dataset is constructed from 2,000 demonstrations covering 28 canonical 18 object categories. Before splitting, we group demonstrations by hashes of their complete state and action sequences to keep identical recorded trajectories within the same partition. We remove robot pixels from the detector inputs and convert visible-instance masks into polygon annotations. frame is discarded if any retained objects polygon has an IoU below 0.90 with its source mask. This filtering removes 182 frames and yields 12,599 training, 1,578 validation, and 1,641 test frames. The test split contains held-out demonstrations with task categories and simulator assets shared with the training split. For CALVIN, we fine-tune the detector directly on scene-D demonstrations using 11 categories covering scene objects and robot parts. We split demonstration episodes before sampling frames and render the recorded robot and scene states to obtain RGB observations and instance annotations. The dataset contains 256 training frames from 24 episodes and 64 validation frames from seven disjoint episodes. All 320 RGB images are unique, and exact RGB matches to the 40 scene-D comparison frames used below are excluded. Polygon annotations retain contours with at least three vertices and an area of at least two pixels. Both adaptations start from the original YOLOE-11L segmentation checkpoint and use AdamW with an input resolution of 640. For LIBERO, we use an initial learning rate of 2 104, batch size of 16, two warm-up epochs, and up to 30 training epochs, with an early-stopping patience of eight epochs. For CALVIN, we use an initial learning rate of 1.5 104, batch size of four, one warm-up epoch, and eight training epochs. We select the checkpoint with the best validation performance for each benchmark. We evaluate the box and mask predictions produced by YOLOE itself in Table 7. Within each benchmark, the original and fine-tuned detectors use the same evaluation images and canonical vocabulary. LIBERO results are computed on the 1,641 held-out test frames retained after polygon-quality filtering, using confidence threshold of 0.001 and non-maximum-suppression IoU threshold of 0.5. CALVIN results are computed on the same 64 scene-D validation frames used for checkpoint selection, with configured non-maximum-suppression IoU threshold of 0.7. Fine-tuning improves all reported box and mask AP metrics under these evaluation protocols. Table 7: Box and mask AP (%) of YOLOE. LIBERO uses 1,641 held-out test frames. sections.title: F Policy Ablation Protocols
sections.content: Table 4 compares the original StarVLA-GR00T backbone, full WeaveVLA, and its three ablated variants on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. The three ablated WeaveVLA variants use the same backbone, training data, optimization budget, and checkpoint-selection rule as the full model. Evaluation uses matched initial states and 500 rollouts per LIBERO suite, while LIBERO-Plus reports pooled success rates across perturbations without additional fine-tuning. Across the full model and its three ablations, perception, tracked identities, TCP anchoring, coverage-weighted appearance pooling, and the original VLM context are kept consistent. Removing geometry reconstruction sets λg = 0, retaining the flow-matching objective and all geometric inputs. The no-edge-memory variant removes the GRU and its pair-specific hidden states. Spatial edge features are passed to the subsequent VLM-conditioning and readout stages without recurrent fusion, while geometry caching and graph connectivity remain unchanged. The full-connectivity variant replaces task-conditioned connections with directed edges between all distinct valid scene nodes, including task-irrelevant objects and the gripper. For valid nodes, this produces (N 1) directed edges without self-loops. No additional ground-truth objects are introduced. Relative geometric descriptors, recurrent edge updates, observation-validity rules, and the remaining model components are preserved. Real-World Evaluation Details Evaluation protocol. The protocol specifies 30 standard trials and 30 perturbed trials per task and method. The perturbed trials allocate ten trials each to table clutter, random lighting, and background variation. sections.title: H Spatial Relations During Manipulation
sections.content: Figure 7: Spatial relations throughout crowded manipulation task. Six observations from successful WeaveVLA rollout track the same gripper, target bowl, plate, and nearby objects. Arrows show selected recorded graph connections, and the dashed orange trace follows the target bowl in the image plane. Figure 7 shows LIBERO-Spatial rollout (task 0, trial 24) in which the robot picks up the black bowl between the plate and the ramekin and places it on the plate. The six panels correspond to control steps 0, 24, 40, 56, 64, and 72. Persistent entity IDs link the target bowl (5), neighboring bowl (3), plate (2), ramekin (7), and gripper (8) across observations. Both black bowls are instruction candidates in the recorded graph. Initially, the target bowl lies between the plate and ramekin in the scene. As the gripper approaches and lifts it, the gripperbowl relation changes along with the bowls position relative to the references. The final panels show the bowl moving toward and overlapping the plate in the image. The displayed arrows are selected directed connections from the graph logs. Colors and the choice of highlighted edges serve illustration. Dashed circles denote cached node locations during missing observations. The overlays use logged image coordinates and depict image-plane spatial relationships.
